claim: Single-particle cryo-EM structure determination is transforming structural biology by reaching near-atomic resolution for a wide range of specimens.
source: By reaching near-atomic resolution for a wide range of specimens, single-particle cryo-EM structure determination is transforming structural biology.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general assertion about the field.

claim: The necessary calculations for cryo-EM structure determination come at large computational costs.
source: However, the necessary calculations come at large computational costs, which has introduced a bottleneck that is currently limiting throughput and the development of new methods.
evidence: This is stated as a problem in the abstract.

claim: Large computational costs have introduced a bottleneck that is currently limiting throughput and the development of new methods in cryo-EM.
source: However, the necessary calculations come at large computational costs, which has introduced a bottleneck that is currently limiting throughput and the development of new methods.
evidence: This is stated as a consequence of computational costs in the abstract.

claim: RELION-2 uses graphics processors (GPUs) to address the most computationally intensive steps of its cryo-EM structure determination workflow.
source: Here, we present an implementation of the RELION image processing software that uses graphics processors (GPUs) to address the most computationally intensive steps of its cryo-EM structure determination workflow.
evidence: This is the main contribution described in the abstract.

claim: Image classification in RELION-2 has been accelerated more than an order-of-magnitude on desktop hardware.
source: Both image classification and high-resolution refinement have been accelerated more than an order-of-magnitude, and template-based particle selection has been accelerated well over two orders-of-magnitude on desktop hardware.
evidence: This is stated as a performance result in the abstract.

claim: High-resolution refinement in RELION-2 has been accelerated more than an order-of-magnitude on desktop hardware.
source: Both image classification and high-resolution refinement have been accelerated more than an order-of-magnitude, and template-based particle selection has been accelerated well over two orders-of-magnitude on desktop hardware.
evidence: This is stated as a performance result in the abstract.

claim: Template-based particle selection in RELION-2 has been accelerated well over two orders-of-magnitude on desktop hardware.
source: Both image classification and high-resolution refinement have been accelerated more than an order-of-magnitude, and template-based particle selection has been accelerated well over two orders-of-magnitude on desktop hardware.
evidence: This is stated as a performance result in the abstract.

claim: Memory requirements on GPUs in RELION-2 have been reduced to fit widely available hardware.
source: Memory requirements on GPUs have been reduced to fit widely available hardware, and we show that the use of single precision arithmetic does not adversely affect results.
evidence: This is stated as an achievement in the abstract.

claim: The use of single precision arithmetic in RELION-2 does not adversely affect results.
source: Memory requirements on GPUs have been reduced to fit widely available hardware, and we show that the use of single precision arithmetic does not adversely affect results.
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the abstract and demonstrated in Figure 5.

claim: RELION-2 enables high-resolution cryo-EM structure determination in a matter of days on a single workstation.
source: This enables high-resolution cryo-EM structure determination in a matter of days on a single workstation.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the abstract and demonstrated with the β-galactosidase workflow.

claim: Direct-electron detectors and advanced methods of image processing have made structural characterisation of macromolecular complexes to near-atomic resolution feasible using single-particle electron cryo-microscopy.
source: With the advent of direct-electron detectors and advanced methods of image processing, structural characterisation of macromolecular complexes to near-atomic resolution is now feasible using single-particle electron cryo-microscopy (cryo-EM) (Cheng, 2015; Fernandez-Leiro and Scheres, 2016b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to other work.

claim: Access to high-end microscopes is limited partly due to the steep increase in demand.
source: First, partly due to the steep increase in demand, access to high-end microscopes is limited.
evidence: This is stated as a known problem in the field.

claim: The limited access to high-end microscopes is being addressed with acquisition of new equipment in a large number of departments worldwide and the establishment of shared infrastructures.
source: This is being addressed with acquisition of new equipment in a large number of departments worldwide, as well as the establishment of shared infrastructures (Saibil et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: Processing the large amounts of data produced by cryo-EM microscopes requires computational hardware that is not directly accessible to many labs.
source: Second, processing the large amounts of data produced by these microscopes requires computational hardware that is not directly accessible to many labs.
evidence: This is stated as a problem in the introduction.

claim: The computational requirements at larger centres are so high that cryo-EM now suffers from a computational bottleneck.
source: Even at larger centres the computational requirements are so high that cryo-EM now suffers from a computational bottleneck.
evidence: This is stated as a problem in the introduction.

claim: A typical cryo-EM data set may constitute hundreds or thousands of images (called micrographs) of a thin layer of vitreous ice in which multiple individual macromolecular complexes (called particles) are imaged.
source: A typical cryo-EM data set may constitute hundreds or thousands of images (called micrographs) of a thin layer of vitreous ice in which multiple individual macromolecular complexes (called particles) are imaged.
evidence: This is a description of typical cryo-EM data.

claim: Radiation damage imposes strict limitations on the electron exposure in cryo-EM.
source: Because radiation damage imposes strict limitations on the electron exposure, micrographs are extremely noisy.
evidence: This is stated as a fundamental constraint in cryo-EM.

claim: Micrographs in cryo-EM are extremely noisy because radiation damage imposes strict limitations on the electron exposure.
source: Because radiation damage imposes strict limitations on the electron exposure, micrographs are extremely noisy.
evidence: This is stated as a consequence of radiation damage.

claim: To extract fine structural details in cryo-EM, one needs to average over multiple images of identical complexes to cancel noise sufficiently.
source: Thus, to extract fine structural details, one needs to average over multiple images of identical complexes to cancel noise sufficiently.
evidence: This is stated as a fundamental principle of cryo-EM.

claim: The regularised likelihood optimisation algorithm in RELION is computationally demanding.
source: Unfortunately, the regularised likelihood optimisation algorithm that underlies these calculations is computationally demanding.
evidence: This is stated as a problem with RELION.

claim: A recent 3.7 Å structure of a yeast spliceosomal complex required more than half a million CPU hours of classification and high-resolution refinement.
source: We estimate that a recent 3.7 Å structure of a yeast spliceosomal complex (Nguyen et al., 2016) required more than half a million CPU hours of classification and high-resolution refinement.
evidence: This is an estimate based on a specific published structure.

claim: Computations of the magnitude required for the yeast spliceosomal complex structure require the use of high-performance computing clusters with dedicated staff.
source: Computations of this magnitude require the use of high-performance computing clusters with dedicated staff, and restrict the exploration of new image processing schemes.
evidence: This is stated as a consequence of the computational requirements.

claim: The introduction of hardware accelerators such as GPUs has recently transformed other scientific fields where computation was a bottleneck.
source: The introduction of hardware accelerators, such as graphics processors (GPUs), has recently transformed other scientific fields where computation was a bottleneck.
evidence: This is stated as context for the work.

claim: To exploit GPU hardware, substantial redesigns of algorithms are required to make many independent tasks simultaneously available for computation.
source: To exploit this type of hardware, substantial redesigns of algorithms are required to make many independent tasks simultaneously available for computation, which is known as exposing (low-level) parallelism.
evidence: This is stated as a requirement for GPU acceleration.

claim: GPU acceleration has been a revolution for molecular dynamics simulations.
source: However, the possible gain is equally substantial; together with commodity hardware it has been a revolution e.g. for molecular dynamics simulations (Salomon-Ferrer et al., 2013; Abraham et al., 2015), quantum chemistry (Ufimtsev and Martínez, 2008), and machine learning (Jia et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: GPU acceleration has been a revolution for quantum chemistry.
source: However, the possible gain is equally substantial; together with commodity hardware it has been a revolution e.g. for molecular dynamics simulations (Salomon-Ferrer et al., 2013; Abraham et al., 2015), quantum chemistry (Ufimtsev and Martínez, 2008), and machine learning (Jia et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: GPU acceleration has been a revolution for machine learning.
source: However, the possible gain is equally substantial; together with commodity hardware it has been a revolution e.g. for molecular dynamics simulations (Salomon-Ferrer et al., 2013; Abraham et al., 2015), quantum chemistry (Ufimtsev and Martínez, 2008), and machine learning (Jia et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: GPU acceleration of computationally expensive algorithms has been performed in other cryo-EM software with varying success and subsequent impact in the field.
source: GPU acceleration of computationally expensive algorithms has also been performed in other cryo-EM software, with varying success and subsequent impact in the field.
evidence: This is stated as context for the work.

claim: Many GPU acceleration attempts in cryo-EM have achieved significant improvement in performance through acceleration of only a few subroutines.
source: Many attempts have achieved significant improvement in performance through acceleration of only a few subroutines (Li et al., 2010; Tagare et al., 2010; Li et al., 2013; Hoang et al., 2013), relieving major bottlenecks.
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Some cryo-EM tools were designed or fundamentally reformulated with particular hardware in mind, which tends to lead to more substantial long-term performance benefits.
source: In contrast, other tools were designed or fundamentally reformulated with a particular hardware in mind (Li et al., 2015; Zhang, 2016); this tends to lead to more substantial long-term performance benefits, and for some steps the accelerated implementations have fully replaced CPU codes.
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: RELION has historically scaled to large resources by using higher-level parallelism, where computational tasks are divided into subsets of particle images in each iterative refinement step.
source: Historically, RELION (like most alternatives) has scaled to the large resources it needs by using higher-level parallelism, where computational tasks are divided into subsets of particle images in each iterative refinement step.
evidence: This is stated as a description of previous RELION implementation.

claim: Lower-level core computations on individual particle images in RELION have remained serialised since its introduction more than four years ago.
source: However, lower-level core computations on individual particle images in RELION have remained serialised since its introduction more than four years ago.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of previous RELION implementation.

claim: The RELION-2 implementation uses GPUs to address computational bottlenecks in the regularised likelihood optimisation algorithm.
source: Here, we describe a new implementation of the regularised likelihood optimisation algorithm in RELION that uses GPUs to address its computational bottlenecks.
evidence: This is stated as the main contribution.

claim: The increased parallelism in RELION-2 was implemented in CUDA, a programming language provided by NVIDIA.
source: We have chosen to implement our increased parallelism in CUDA, a programming language provided by NVIDIA.
evidence: This is stated as an implementation choice.

claim: The CUDA language currently dominates the GPU computing market.
source: The CUDA language currently dominates the GPU computing market, and provides a stable programming environment with a rich C++ interface.
evidence: This is stated as justification for using CUDA.

claim: RELION-2 utilises cuFFT for fast Fourier transforms.
source: We also utilise a number of libraries provided within the CUDA framework, such as cuFFT for fast Fourier transforms (FFTs), and CUB/thrust for sorting and other standard functions.
evidence: This is stated as an implementation detail.

claim: RELION-2 utilises CUB/thrust for sorting and other standard functions.
source: We also utilise a number of libraries provided within the CUDA framework, such as cuFFT for fast Fourier transforms (FFTs), and CUB/thrust for sorting and other standard functions.
evidence: This is stated as an implementation detail.

claim: There is wide availability of cheap consumer hardware that supports CUDA, which provides outstanding value for many research groups.
source: In addition to high-end professional cards there is wide availability of cheap consumer hardware that supports CUDA, which provides outstanding value for many research groups.
evidence: This is stated as a benefit of using CUDA.

claim: The acceleration in RELION-2 addresses the most computationally intensive steps in a typical image processing workflow, including 2D or 3D classification and 3D auto-refine.
source: The present acceleration of relion addresses the most computationally intensive steps in a typical image processing workflow. This includes classification of data into structurally homogeneous subsets (2D or 3D classification) and high-resolution refinement of each homogeneous such set of particles (3D auto-refine).
evidence: This is stated as a description of what was accelerated.

claim: RELION-2 includes an improved algorithm for semi-automated selection of particles from micrographs that targets GPUs.
source: In addition, we describe an improved algorithm for semi-automated selection of particles from micrographs (Scheres, 2015), this too targeting GPUs.
evidence: This is stated as an additional contribution.

claim: The regularised likelihood optimisation in RELION uses an Expectation-Maximization algorithm to find the most likely 3D density map for a large set of 2D particle images with unknown orientations.
source: The regularised likelihood optimisation in relion uses an Expectation-Maximization algorithm (Dempster et al., 1977) to find the most likely 3D density map for a large set of 2D particles images with unknown orientations, under the prior expectation that the 3D map has limited power in the Fourier domain.
evidence: This is a description of the algorithm with a citation.

claim: The Expectation-Maximization algorithm in RELION involves two fundamental steps at every iteration: the E-step and the M-step.
source: This iterative algorithm involves two fundamental steps at every iteration. In the expectation, or E-step, one calculates probability distributions for the relative orientations of all particles based on the current estimate of the 3D map. In the subsequent maximization, or M-step, one updates the estimate for the 3D map.
evidence: This is a description of the algorithm.

claim: In the E-step, one calculates probability distributions for the relative orientations of all particles based on the current estimate of the 3D map.
source: In the expectation, or E-step, one calculates probability distributions for the relative orientations of all particles based on the current estimate of the 3D map.
evidence: This is a description of the E-step.

claim: In the M-step, one updates the estimate for the 3D map.
source: In the subsequent maximization, or M-step, one updates the estimate for the 3D map.
evidence: This is a description of the M-step.

claim: The E-step in RELION requires four major computational stages: projection of the 3D reference map, calculation of differences between reference projections and particle images, conversion of differences to probability-weights, and back-projection of weighted particle images.
source: Within a single iteration, the E-step requires four major computational stages (Figure 1): (i) The current 3D reference map is projected along many orientations; (ii) the difference between these reference projections and every particle image is calculated for each orientation and for each sampled translation; (iii) all these differences are converted to probability-weights; and (iv) those weights are used to update a running sum of the back-projected particle images in 3D Fourier space.
evidence: This is described in the text and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Operations (i), (ii) and (iv) of the E-step have dominated execution time in previous versions of RELION.
source: Therefore, operations (i), (ii) and (iv) of the E-step have dominated execution time in previous versions of RELION.
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of previous RELION versions.

claim: Modern accelerator processors such as GPUs achieve very high floating-point performance by incorporating a large set (thousands) of very simple and streamlined functional units.
source: Modern accelerator processors - such as GPUs - achieve very high floating-point performance by incorporating a large set (thousands) of very simple and streamlined functional units instead of the handful advanced general-purpose cores in a normal (CPU) processor.
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of GPU hardware.

claim: Previous versions of RELION scaled over multiple CPU cores by using separate processes for independent particle images.
source: In previous versions, RELION has scaled over multiple CPU cores by using separate processes for independent particle images.
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of previous RELION versions.

claim: GPUs require much broader low-level parallelism to increase performance substantially.
source: GPUs however require much broader low-level parallelism to increase performance substantially.
evidence: This is stated as a requirement for GPU acceleration.

claim: The RELION-2 implementation treats multiple reference maps, all relative image translations and orientations, and even individual image pixels as parallel tasks.
source: By treating multiple reference maps, all relative image translations and orientations, and even individual image pixels as parallel tasks (Figure 2), we created sufficient low-level parallelism to provide outstanding performance on accelerator hardware such as GPUs.
evidence: This is described in the text and illustrated in Figure 2.

claim: The RELION-2 implementation stores a two-fold oversampled Fourier transform of each reference in GPU memory, and 2D slices are extracted only when needed.
source: Instead, like the CPU code, our implementation stores a two-fold oversampled Fourier transform of each reference in GPU memory, and 2D slices (along any orientation) are extracted only when needed.
evidence: This is stated as an implementation detail.

claim: GPU textures are well-suited for the resampling operations when taking slices from the 3D Fourier transform in RELION-2.
source: In RELION, they turn out to be well-suited for the resampling operations when taking slices from the 3D Fourier transform.
evidence: This is stated as a finding about the implementation.

claim: The CPU version of RELION has historically used double precision.
source: Finally, like most scientific software, the CPU version of relion has historically used double precision, and merely recompiling in single does not improve performance.
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of previous RELION versions.

claim: All GPUs provide higher performance for single precision compared to double precision.
source: However, all GPUs provide higher performance for single precision, and the dedicated texture units can typically only perform reduced-precision operations.
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of GPU hardware.

claim: The E-step in RELION-2 was reformulated to be less precision-sensitive, making it possible to execute these calculations in single precision without adverse effects on the final results.
source: For these reasons we also reformulated our implementation of the E-step to be less precision-sensitive, making it possible to execute these calculations in single precision without adverse effects on the final results.
evidence: This is stated as an implementation choice and validated in Figure 5.

claim: The M-step in RELION-2 remains on the CPU and is still executed in double precision.
source: As we did not accelerate the M-step, this part of the algorithm remains on the CPU and is still executed in double precision.
evidence: This is stated as an implementation detail.

claim: RELION implements a template-based particle selection procedure that calculates a probability measure (the R-value) for each pixel in the micrograph.
source: RELION also implements a template-based particle selection procedure, which calculates a probability measure (the R-value) for each pixel in the micrograph to signify the likelihood that it is the location of any of the provided templates (Scheres, 2015).
evidence: This is a description of the particle selection procedure with a citation.

claim: The R-value map of a micrograph considers all possible rotations of each template.
source: The R-value map of a micrograph considers all possible rotations of each template, and is subsequently used in a peak-search algorithm that locates particles within the original micrograph (Figure 3).
evidence: This is described in the text and illustrated in Figure 3.

claim: In the particle selection procedure, execution time becomes negligible compared to the time spent performing FFTs to transform image objects between real and Fourier spaces.
source: In fact, they are so fast that their execution time becomes negligible compared to the time spent performing FFTs to transform image objects between real and Fourier spaces.
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of the particle selection procedure.

claim: In the GPU version of particle selection, 72 inverse FFTs are performed concurrently on the GPU when using 5-degree incremental template rotations.
source: For example, when using 5-degree incremental template rotations, 72 such inverse FFTs are now performed concurrently on the GPU through the cufft cuda library.
evidence: This is stated as an implementation detail.

claim: The performance of RELION-2 on a workstation equipped with modern GPUs can exceed that of hundreds of CPU cores.
source: The performance of our implementation on a workstation equipped with modern GPUs can exceed that of hundreds of CPU cores (Figure 4).
evidence: This is stated as a result and shown in Figure 4.

claim: Calculations where many classes and orientations need to be sampled experience the greatest gain from the GPU acceleration in RELION-2.
source: This is most prominent for increasing numbers of pixels, orientations and classes, due to the increased low-level parallelism RELION-2 has been designed to use efficiently. Therefore, calculations where many classes and orientations need to be sampled, e.g. 3D classifications over multiple classes and with fine sampling of orientations, experience the greatest gain from the acceleration (Figure 4).
evidence: This is stated as a result and shown in Figure 4.

claim: For sufficiently large computational problems, RELION's processing time scales linearly with increased number of classes.
source: For sufficiently large computational problems, relion's processing time scales linearly with increased number of classes, but since the extra calculations are much faster with the GPU-enabled version the relative advantage is larger the more classes are used (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is stated as a result and shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The calculations still performed on the CPU dominate both the execution and scaling even for the GPU version of RELION-2.
source: Further scrutiny reveals that the calculations still performed on the CPU actually dominate both the execution and scaling even for the GPU version (Figure 4E), which indicates new bottlenecks are now limiting scaling - we intend to focus on these parts of the code for future improvements.
evidence: This is stated as a finding and shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Two double-precision CPU refinements using different random seeds produce distributions where 81% of images fall within 1° of the other.
source: Two double-precision CPU refinements (using different random seeds) produce distributions where 81% of images fall within 1∘ of the other.
evidence: This is stated as a result of comparing CPU refinements.

claim: The single-precision GPU implementation finds 82% of images within 1° tolerance compared to a CPU refinement.
source: The single-precision GPU implementation finds 82% of images within the same 1∘ tolerance. (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated as a result and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The differences in image orientations due to random seeds are at least as large as any systematic variation between the CPU and GPU versions of RELION.
source: In other words, the differences due to random seeds are at least as large as any systematic variation between the CPU and GPU versions.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the results.

claim: The assignments of image orientations in single-precision GPU implementation are similar enough to not influence the final reconstruction quality.
source: While a small loss of precision was observed e.g. in the fast interpolation (texture) intrinsics, the assignments of image orientations are similar enough to not influence the final reconstruction quality (Figure 5).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion and shown in Figure 5.

claim: Single-precision execution of the iterative gridding algorithm that underlies the reconstruction in the M-step exhibited a notable deviation from the double-precision version when first tested.
source: In contrast, single-precision execution of the iterative gridding algorithm that underlies the reconstruction in the M-step (Scheres, 2012a) did exhibit a notable deviation from the double-precision version when first tested.
evidence: This is stated as a finding during development.

claim: RELION-2 uses a hybrid implementation where the E-step is performed in single precision on the GPU while the M-step remains in double precision on the CPU.
source: Therefore, we opted for a hybrid implementation of the algorithm: The computationally demanding slice projections, probability calculations, and back-projections in the E-step are performed in single precision on the GPU, while the reconstruction in the M-step remains in double precision on the CPU.
evidence: This is stated as an implementation choice.

claim: RELION has traditionally required large amounts of memory.
source: relion has traditionally required large amounts of memory.
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of RELION.

claim: Peak memory use in RELION occurs during the M-step, which is executed on the CPU using the gridding reconstruction algorithm.
source: Fortunately its peak use is however not during the accelerated, computationally most intensive, parts of the algorithm. Rather, memory use peaks during the M-step, which is executed on the CPU using the gridding reconstruction algorithm mentioned above.
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of RELION's memory usage.

claim: When resolving detail at the Nyquist frequency, RELION requires memory corresponding to twice the cube of the image dimension due to twofold oversampling.
source: When resolving detail at the Nyquist frequency, due to a twofold oversampling (associated with gridding during reconstruction), relion requires memory corresponding to twice the cube of the image dimension.
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of RELION's memory requirements.

claim: For 400²-pixel particle images, RELION requires a grid size of 800³, which becomes ~2 GB per class in single precision.
source: For example, when using 4002-pixel particle images, the required grid size is 8003, which becomes ∼2 GB per class, since each value requires 4 bytes in single precision.
evidence: This is stated as an example calculation.

claim: At most 6 GB of GPU memory is needed to perform refinement to Nyquist with image sizes up to 400².
source: In practice, memory use with image sizes up to 4002 indicate that at most 6 GB of GPU memory is needed to perform refinement to Nyquist (Figure 6).
evidence: This is stated as a practical finding and shown in Figure 6.

claim: Classification using 3D references is usually performed at resolutions much lower than the Nyquist limit, and for this reason its memory requirements are typically much lower.
source: Classification using 3D references is usually performed at resolutions much lower than the Nyquist limit, and for this reason its memory requirements are typically much lower.
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of 3D classification.

claim: Because of the much improved performance in RELION-2, multiple tasks have become limited by how fast input data can be read from disk.
source: In addition, because of the much improved performance, multiple tasks have become limited by how fast input data can be read from disk.
evidence: This is stated as a consequence of the acceleration.

claim: It is highly beneficial to explicitly cache data on local solid state devices (SSDs) in RELION-2.
source: Therefore, we now find it highly beneficial to explicitly cache data on local solid state devices (SSDs), as has also been observed for GPU-accelerated CTF estimation (Zhang, 2016).
evidence: This is stated as a finding with a citation.

claim: RELION-2 features the ability to automatically copy data sets to fast local disks prior to refinement.
source: To allow this in a straightforward way, RELION-2 features the ability to automatically copy data sets to fast local disks prior to refinement, which further increases performance during less computationally intensive steps, such as 2D classification.
evidence: This is stated as a new feature.

claim: The cross-correlation-based particle selection in RELION is dominated by computing many large inverse FFTs.
source: Even after parallelisation and acceleration on GPUs, the cross-correlation-based particle selection in relion is dominated by computing many large inverse FFTs (Figure 3), as has been observed previously for similar methods (Castaño-Díez et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated as a finding with a citation and shown in Figure 3.

claim: Little difference was found in the particles selected when discarding resolution information in micrographs beyond that of search templates.
source: We found little difference in the particles selected when discarding resolution information in micrographs beyond that of search templates.
evidence: This is stated as a finding.

claim: Low-pass filtering of micrographs drastically reduces the size of FFT grids and subsequent computations, providing large acceleration at virtually no quality loss.
source: While intuitively straightforward, this conclusion drastically reduces the size of FFT grids and subsequent computations, which provides large acceleration at virtually no quality loss.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the finding.

claim: Low-pass filtering significantly reduces the amount of memory required for particle selection.
source: The low-pass filtering also significantly reduces the amount of memory required for particle selection, which permits parallelism to target hardware like desktop workstations more efficiently.
evidence: This is stated as a benefit of low-pass filtering.

claim: The β-galactosidase benchmark (EMPIAR entry 10017) consists of 84 micrographs of 4096² pixels (1.77 Å/pixel) with coordinates for 40,863 manually selected particles.
source: We further evaluated the quality of filtered selection according to the β-galactosidase benchmark (EMPIAR entry 10017) used in the original implementation in RELION-1.3 (Scheres, 2015). This data set consists of 84 micrographs of 40962 pixels (1.77 Å/pixel), and comes with coordinates for 40,863 particles that were manually selected by Richard Henderson.
evidence: This is a description of the benchmark dataset with a citation.

claim: Filtered selection did not decrease the quality of the autopicking results for the β-galactosidase benchmark.
source: Filtered selection did not decrease the quality of the results, but provided a just-so-slightly increased recall without increasing the false discovery rate (FDR, see e.g. (Langlois and Frank, 2011) for definitions of recall and FDR).
evidence: This is stated as a result with a citation for definitions.

claim: When filtering and GPU-acceleration are combined, a single GPU provides roughly 120 times the performance of an 8-core desktop for autopicking.
source: When filtering and GPU-acceleration are combined, a single GPU provides roughly 120 times the performance of an 8-core desktop, and the desktop can easily be equipped with quad GPUs for about 500x performance gain.
evidence: This is stated as a result.

claim: A desktop can easily be equipped with quad GPUs for about 500x performance gain in autopicking.
source: When filtering and GPU-acceleration are combined, a single GPU provides roughly 120 times the performance of an 8-core desktop, and the desktop can easily be equipped with quad GPUs for about 500x performance gain.
evidence: This is stated as a result.

claim: The semi-automated particle picking in RELION-2 can become limited by disk access unless data is read from an SSD.
source: In fact, similarly to the regularised likelihood optimisation, the semi-automated particle picking can become limited by disk access unless data is read from an SSD.
evidence: This is stated as a finding.

claim: The EMPIAR-10061 dataset of β-galactosidase represents the largest presently available dataset in the EMPIAR database.
source: To illustrate the impact of our GPU implementation and show how it can alter practical work, we chose to re-analyse the EMPIAR-10061 dataset of β-galactosidase (Bartesaghi et al., 2015) using RELION-2. This represents the largest presently available dataset in the empiar database, and provides a realistic challenge.
evidence: This is stated as justification for choosing this dataset with a citation.

claim: Calculating a β-galactosidase map to 2.2 Å resolution using RELION-2 took a few days on a single workstation with four GTX 1080 cards.
source: Calculating a map to 2.2 Å resolution (Figure 8A) took a few days – comparable to, if not faster than, the time required acquire this amount of high-quality data.
evidence: This is stated as a result and shown in Figure 8A.

claim: The time to calculate a 2.2 Å resolution β-galactosidase map using RELION-2 is comparable to, if not faster than, the time required to acquire this amount of high-quality data.
source: Calculating a map to 2.2 Å resolution (Figure 8A) took a few days – comparable to, if not faster than, the time required acquire this amount of high-quality data.
evidence: This is stated as a comparison.

claim: The parts of the RELION-2 workflow that have been GPU-accelerated no longer dominate execution, exposing other new bottlenecks.
source: The parts of the workflow that have been GPU-accelerated no longer dominate execution, but this exposes other new bottlenecks.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the complete workflow analysis.

claim: Steps that involve reading large movie files from disk become problematic in the RELION-2 workflow.
source: In particular, steps that involve reading large movie files from disk become problematic.
evidence: This is stated as a specific bottleneck.

claim: The β-galactosidase complex used for the benchmark is rigid in nature.
source: We also note that due to the rigid nature of the β-galactosidase complex used for this benchmark, only a single 3D classification was performed.
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of the benchmark.

claim: Typically 3D classification is repeated multiple times to identify, sort, and isolate structural heterogeneity in cryo-EM workflows.
source: This is not representative for many other use cases: typically 3D classification is repeated multiple times to identify, sort, and isolate structural heterogeneity.
evidence: This is stated as typical practice in cryo-EM.

claim: In scenarios with increased or multiple 3D classifications, the impact of the GPU acceleration is even larger.
source: In such a scenario, the impact of the GPU acceleration is even larger, as increased or multiple 3D classifications would still not dominate the complete workflow.
evidence: This is stated as an inference about typical use cases.

claim: The principal benefits of RELION-2 are twofold: lowering the threshold for trial, error and successive improvement of existing methods, and enabling cryo-EM processing with much less hardware.
source: The principal benefits drawn from the presented work are twofold. First, the nature of progress in scientific applications is to continually re-evaluate and examine data in many different ways. With ease of re-processing data, the threshold for trial, error and successive improvement of existing methods is now markedly lowered. Second, the order-of-magnitude speedups make it possible to get by with much less hardware for cryo-EM processing, in most cases even desktops.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of benefits.

claim: The order-of-magnitude speedups in RELION-2 remove a computational bottleneck for large labs.
source: This removes a computational bottleneck for large labs, and enables any group to perform their own reconstruction without access to supercomputers.
evidence: This is stated as a benefit.

claim: RELION-2 enables any group to perform their own reconstruction without access to supercomputers.
source: This removes a computational bottleneck for large labs, and enables any group to perform their own reconstruction without access to supercomputers.
evidence: This is stated as a benefit.

claim: Larger data sets and image sizes are expected in the next few years in cryo-EM.
source: In the next few years, larger data sets and image sizes are expected, as well as new methods that require expedient processing of large data sets.
evidence: This is stated as an expectation about the field.

claim: The large reduction in computational costs in RELION-2 opens up the possibility to perform more ambitious computational analyses without increasing the investments.
source: The large reduction in computational costs opens up the possibility to perform more ambitious computational analyses without increasing the investments.
evidence: This is stated as a consequence of the work.

claim: The favourable scaling of performance for multi-class refinements will make it feasible to use many more classes than was practical before.
source: For example, the favourable scaling of performance we observed for multi-class refinements will make it feasible to use many more classes than was practical before, which will lead to better descriptions of conformational diversity in flexible molecules.
evidence: This is stated as an expected benefit.

claim: Using many more classes in multi-class refinements will lead to better descriptions of conformational diversity in flexible molecules.
source: For example, the favourable scaling of performance we observed for multi-class refinements will make it feasible to use many more classes than was practical before, which will lead to better descriptions of conformational diversity in flexible molecules.
evidence: This is stated as an expected benefit.

claim: With even faster algorithms and hardware it might soon be possible to perform highly automated, on-the-fly, structure determination while data acquisition is ongoing.
source: Additionally, with even faster algorithms and hardware it might soon be possible to perform highly automated, on-the-fly, structure determination while data acquisition is ongoing.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation about future possibilities.

claim: RELION-2 already implements a pipelined approach for automated execution of pre-determined image processing workflows.
source: In anticipation of these developments, RELION-2 already implements a pipelined approach for automated execution of pre-determined image processing workflows (Fernandez-Leiro and Scheres, 2016a).
evidence: This is stated as a feature with a citation.

claim: The large speedup in RELION-2 has exposed several new areas of the code that can now dominate execution time, such as data input/output and the reconstruction step.
source: While the new GPU implementation has removed many of the previous computational bottlenecks in relion, the large speedup has exposed several new areas of the code that can now dominate execution time, such as data input/output and the reconstruction step during iterative image refinement.
evidence: This is stated as a finding.

claim: In some cases, data input/output and the reconstruction step now collectively account for roughly 50% of total execution time in RELION-2.
source: Although these parts of the algorithm were previously insignificant, in some cases they now collectively account for roughly 50% of total execution time.
evidence: This is stated as a finding.

claim: Future work on RELION will strive to further generalise parallelism such that performance is less dependent on the type of refinement performed.
source: Future work will e.g. strive to further generalise parallelism such that performance is less dependent on the type of refinement performed, as sufficient parallelism is always available within the relion core algorithm.
evidence: This is stated as a plan for future work.

claim: Memory requirements on the GPU are expected to be reduced further in future versions of RELION.
source: Memory requirements on the GPU are also expected to be reduced further, so that larger image sizes and more classes can be handled to higher resolution.
evidence: This is stated as a plan for future work.

claim: With the current implementation, cryo-EM structures to near-atomic resolution can be calculated in a matter of days on a single workstation, or hours on a GPU-cluster.
source: With the current implementation, cryo-EM structures to near-atomic resolution can be calculated in a matter of days on a single workstation, or hours on a GPU-cluster.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of capabilities.

claim: The aim of the current adaptations is not to present a final solution to computational needs in RELION.
source: Nevertheless, the aim of the current adaptations is not to present a final solution to computational needs in RELION; while the present version achieves excellent speedup on a wide range of low-cost systems, we expect the acceleration to improve both in performance and coverage.
evidence: This is stated as a clarification of the work's scope.

claim: Generalising the low-level parallelism in RELION-2 to vectorised CPU calculations and possibly OpenCL will constitute little more than translating this parallelism to new instructions.
source: Generalising the low-level parallelism described here to vectorised CPU calculations, and possibly an open GPU language like OpenCL, will constitute little more than translating this parallelism to new instructions.
evidence: This is stated as a plan for future work.

claim: RELION 2 is both open source and free software, distributed under the GPLv2 licence.
source: RELION 2 is both open source and free software, distributed under the GPLv2 licence.
evidence: This is stated as a fact about the software.

claim: RELION 2 is publicly available for download through http://www2.mrc-lmb.cam.ac.uk/relion.
source: It is publicly available for download through http://www2.mrc-lmb.cam.ac.uk/relion.
evidence: This is stated as a fact about software availability.

claim: The acceleration in RELION-2 works with any NVIDIA GPU of compute-capability 3.5 or higher.
source: The acceleration in RELION-2 works with any NVIDIA GPU of compute-capability 3.5 or higher, which covers all models launched the last three years.
evidence: This is stated as a hardware requirement.

claim: Version 7.0 of the CUDA toolkit is required for RELION-2 and was used for all presented results.
source: Version 7.0 of the CUDA toolkit is also required, and was used for all presented results.
evidence: This is stated as a software requirement.

claim: Hyperthreading was enabled and used for all CPU benchmarks because it improves performance on the CPU side slightly.
source: While we refer to the physical core count when describing hardware, hyperthreading was enabled and used for all benchmarks (i.e., starting 560 threads on the 10 nodes) since it improves performance on the CPU side slightly.
evidence: This is stated as a methodological detail.

claim: In all cases where different hardware and/or software implementations were compared, identical refinement parameters were used, including the random seed provided to RELION.
source: In all cases where different hardware and/or software implementations were compared, identical refinement parameters were used, including the random seed provided to RELION.
evidence: This is stated as a methodological detail.

claim: The nondeterministic scheduling and summations of GPU-enabled execution can introduce some minor noise in results.
source: The nondeterministic scheduling and summations of GPU-enabled execution can introduce some minor noise in results, but all runs achieve convergence and variations in final results are well within estimated errors and resolution of the raw data.
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of GPU execution.

claim: All GPU runs achieve convergence and variations in final results are well within estimated errors and resolution of the raw data.
source: The nondeterministic scheduling and summations of GPU-enabled execution can introduce some minor noise in results, but all runs achieve convergence and variations in final results are well within estimated errors and resolution of the raw data.
evidence: This is stated as a finding about GPU execution.

claim: Autopicking with six templates yielded an initial data set of 130,375 particles for the β-galactosidase workflow.
source: Autopicking with six templates yielded an initial data set of 130,375 particles, which were subjected to reference-free 2D classification using 200 classes.
evidence: This is stated as a result from the workflow.

claim: Selection of the 75 best classes from 2D classification resulted in 120,514 particles for the β-galactosidase workflow.
source: Selection of the 75 best classes resulted in 120,514 particles.
evidence: This is stated as a result from the workflow.

claim: Selection of the seven best classes from 3D classification yielded a final data set of 109,963 particles for the β-galactosidase workflow.
source: Selection of the seven best classes yielded a final data set of 109,963 particles, which were submitted to 3D auto-refinement.
evidence: This is stated as a result from the workflow.

claim: The final resolution of the β-galactosidase map was estimated using phase-randomisation to account for the convolution effects of a solvent mask on the FSC between the two independently refined half-maps.
source: The final resolution was estimated using phase-randomisation to account for the convolution effects of a solvent mask on the FSC between the two independently refined half-maps (Chen et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as a methodological detail with a citation.

claim: A quad-GPU workstation easily outperforms even a large cluster job in 3D classification.
source: A quad-GPU workstation easily outperforms even a large cluster job in 3D classification.
evidence: This is stated as a result shown in Figure 4A.

claim: In 2D classification, the GPU desktop performs slightly better in the first few iterations and then provides performance equivalent to the 280 CPU cores.
source: In 2D classification, the GPU desktop performs slightly better in the first few iteration and then provides performance equivalent to the 280 CPU cores.
evidence: This is stated as a result shown in Figure 4B.

claim: A high-resolution refinement of the Plasmodium falciparum 80S ribosome using single precision GPU arithmetic achieves a gold-standard FSC indistinguishable from double precision CPU-only refinement.
source: A high-resolution refinement of the Plasmodium falciparum 80S ribosome using single precision GPU arithmetic achieves a gold-standard Fourier shell correlation (FSC) indistinguishable from double precision CPU-only refinement (previously deposited as EMD-2660).
evidence: This is stated as a result shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The FSC of full reconstructions comparing CPU and GPU methods shows their agreement far exceeds the recoverable signal.
source: The FSC of full reconstructions comparing the two methods shows their agreement far exceeds the recoverable signal (grey), and as shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 the variation in angle assignments match the differences between CPU runs with different random seeds.
evidence: This is stated as a result shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The required GPU memory scales linearly with the number of classes.
source: The required GPU memory scales linearly with the number of classes.
evidence: This is stated as a result shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The maximum required GPU memory occurs for single-class refinement to the Nyquist frequency, which increases rapidly with the image size.
source: The maximum required GPU memory occurs for single-class refinement to the Nyquist frequency, which increases rapidly with the image size.
evidence: This is stated as a result shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Despite near-identical particle selection, performance is dramatically improved with filtering and GPU acceleration.
source: Despite near-identical particle selection, performance is dramatically improved.
evidence: This is stated as a result shown in Figure 7B-C.

claim: Filtering alone provides almost 20-fold performance improvement on any hardware compared to previous versions of RELION.
source: Filtering alone provides almost 20-fold performance improvement on any hardware compared to previsos versions of relion, and when combined with GPU-accelerated particle picking the resulting performance gain is more than two orders of magnitude using only a single GPU (GTX 1080).
evidence: This is stated as a result shown in Figure 7D.

claim: When filtering is combined with GPU-accelerated particle picking, the resulting performance gain is more than two orders of magnitude using only a single GPU (GTX 1080).
source: Filtering alone provides almost 20-fold performance improvement on any hardware compared to previsos versions of relion, and when combined with GPU-accelerated particle picking the resulting performance gain is more than two orders of magnitude using only a single GPU (GTX 1080).
evidence: This is stated as a result shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The resulting 2.2 Å β-galactosidase map shows excellent high-resolution density throughout the complex.
source: The resulting 2.2 Å map (deposited as EMD-4116) shows excellent high-resolution density throughout the complex.
evidence: This is stated as a result shown in Figure 8A.

claim: The total time of image processing for the β-galactosidase workflow was less than that of downloading the data.
source: The total time of image processing was less than that of downloading the data.
evidence: This is stated as a result shown in Figure 8B.
